title: The Count at the Low Gate
passages:
The Stair shut behind them like a door in a house where nobody lived anymore, and after that it was the reach: six miles of drowned suburb with the squall stacked up black over the Kettle at the far end, close enough now that the swell came at them from astern instead of the side.

Bayo stood in the bow with his hands wrapped in strips torn off somebody's shirt, the burns showing through in two dark patches. Dey held the bow line for him, because Bayo couldn't.

"Stump, starboard bow, big as a bus."

"Got it."

"Roof," Bayo said. "Only a roof."

"There's never nothing under a roof," Dey said.

"Nineteen years I've called this reach and held my own line doing it." Bayo said it to the water, then turned and said it to the wheelhouse, loud, so it was on the record of everybody's ears. "Not anymore. My hands are done. I call water and nothing else from here, and you'll not have to guess at it later."

"Noted," Sol said, without looking round. "Keep calling."

Off the port quarter the old road ran down into the brown in long flat steps, each one a fathom, and where the steps quit there was the spoke-box — a traffic circle from before, eight arms of road still standing a hand's width proud of slack water. Wren lobbed the cork floats into it, two bark discs the size of saucers, and the whole deck watched which way the ebb took them.

"Coming back at us," she said.

"Then the hub's turning and we're on the wrong side of it." Bayo pointed with a bandaged finger, which was the most his hands could do. "Mid-channel. Take the middle and let the ebb carry you down."

"We go inside the red," Sol said.

"Inside the red is shoal."

"Inside the red is a fathom more water than the middle, and a fathom is what I'm buying." She put the wheel over. The Marrow leaned, the floats swept by the hull going the other way, and that was the argument finished. "Wren, get inboard of the frame."

Mara was lashed at the wrists in the lift-frame with her chin up, counting. "Sixty-one. Sixty-two." A pause, pleasant as weather. "Somebody's rope."

Nia stood at the rail with the orange wand held against her ribs, warming nothing, and her face went flat the way it did.

The low gate was an arch of poured concrete with a grate under it, forty feet of welded plate and rebar hanging on four chains, and the chains were paying out a notch at a time while the season bell in the tower above rang. Bayo counted the tolls, since counting was what he had instead of hands.

"Six. Three to a shutting."

"Boom," Sol said.

Dey hit the release and the cargo boom came down across the deck with a bang that went through the whole boat, and under the counter, below, Teo slept through it. They slid under the grate with the plate a foot above the wheelhouse, and the chains took another notch behind them, and outside the arch the reach turned white where the squall finally got to it.

Inside was a stone basin, a floating stage, one lantern on a pole. The dock-warden was already at the counter with the berth book open under her hand, and she did not wait for the bow line to be made fast.

"You're one short," Pru Quill said. "The book ends a soul short, and if it ends that way my own berth is forfeit. I'll not round it and I'll not sit on it till morning."

Quill hooked the lantern over the edge of the book to steady it, because the stage was moving on the swell and she was not going to write crooked.

"*Marrow.* Out of the Stair, in on the seventh toll." The pencil was a stub the length of her thumb, held in her fist like a knife. "Master."

"Sol Ferreira."

"Ferreira." She wrote it. "Diver."

"Dey Okafor," Dey said, chin up, like he was volunteering for something worse.

"Okafor." Write. "Topside."

"Wren Achebe."

The pencil stopped. "You're the slate reader."

"I rebuild hours," Wren said. "When people let me."

"Deckhand," Quill said, and Bayo said "Bayo Adisa" before she had finished asking. She wrote Bayo Adisa, then looked at the gap after it where a mark goes. "No mark."

"No mark," Bayo agreed, warm as a hand on your shoulder, like he was giving her something.

"There's a child below," Quill said. "I heard him breathing when your boom came down. I'll have him at this counter before I close."

"He's twelve and he's asleep," Nia said.

"Then he can wake up and be twelve here."

Past the arch the squall had gone from black to a grey with rain in it. Nobody looked at it twice. Quill turned to the last ruled line on the page.

"Name."

Mara had her chin up, watching the chains pay out. "Seventy-eight," she said. "Somebody's rope."

"Mara Vos," Nia said.

"Not off you." Quill didn't raise her voice. She'd no need. "The book takes a name out of the mouth it belongs to. Anything else is a rumour, and I don't write rumours."

"Seventy-nine." Then, to Nia, kindly, the way you'd answer a stranger who'd stopped you in the street to ask the way: "Is it your rope?"

Nia's jaw did something. Dey put a hand on her shoulder and she let him leave it there.

"Write it how she said it," Wren said. "Mara Vos. I'll stand to it. I've her daughter's slate, I've the Caller's spool, I've fourteen months of a man saying it in the dark—"

"Two of you can't hold one line. One soul, one line." The pencil did not move. "And I'll not take a name handed to me like a coat."

"Put mine against hers, then," Bayo said. "Surety. I'll sign for her keep."

"Surety's a debt. This book counts bodies, and a debt doesn't ride up in the cage."

"There's four hundred women in the Kettle," Dey said. "Write *woman*. That's accurate."

"It's a description. I had a description in this book once and it cost me a winter." She looked up, and she looked at Mara properly for the first time, the way you look at a knot you're going to have to pick out of a wet line. "I've no patience for a woman being coy with her own name, either. No name, no line. No line, nothing goes up out of this basin. Not a crate, not a chair, not her. She sits on my stage till the spring bell with the water coming up to the counter, and I will not invent her a name to save my own berth."

Salas stood at the frame with one hand on the rope. He hadn't spoken since the Stair. He didn't speak now.

The bell went. Inside the basin it came flat and doubled, off all that concrete, and above the arch the chain took its notch and the plate came down with a noise like a boiler settling. The gap of grey light under it went from a hand's width to less.

"Two gone," Bayo said. "One left in the chain."

"Eighty," Mara said, pleasant as weather. "Somebody's rope."

Quill turned the book a quarter so the lantern light fell across it, and Wren saw there were three ruled columns where she'd expected two. Name. Berth. Keep.

"What's the third one?"

"What the body carried up," Quill said. "The Kettle doesn't berth what it can't count. Some diver goes down whole and comes up light, I want that in ink, because by spring that same diver is stood on a fourth-tier stairwell with no idea which door is hers, and the house will want to know it was told." She licked the pencil stub. "Ferreira. Keep."

"I'm running a boat," Sol said.

"You're standing at my counter."

"Short," Sol said. "An hour I lost and got back, and I know what was in it. Put that down."

Quill wrote: *knows what she lost.* "Okafor."

"One scrubber, given away," Dey said. "A scrubber is the thing that scrubs the bad out of what you breathe, so you can stay down past where you ought to. Teo's breathing through it now."

"Lungs, then. Not cleared." Write. "Adisa."

"Hands," Bayo said.

"Hands," Quill said, and wrote it, and the pencil went on down the page without her, because that was how the pencil worked. It stopped at the old diver standing at the lift-frame with one hand on the rope. "I'll come to him. He's not going anywhere he can help."

"Achebe," she said. "Keep."

"Nothing worth a column."

"Everything's worth the column. That's why there's a column."

"Then write that I'm topside and I came up dry."

"I don't write what people would rather," Quill said. "I've tried it. It doesn't hold."

The rain got to the stage then, all at once, a hiss across the planks, and Quill lifted the book onto a crate without looking away from Wren's face.

"Eleven seconds," Wren said.

"Eleven seconds of what?"

"That's the whole answer, that's the funny part. I put them in a brass bell at slack water to buy a woman's voice back for her kids, and the toll for paying is you don't keep knowing what you were keeping them for."

The pencil went. Then Quill read it back, flat, the way a woman reads a cargo list, to a deck with six people on it and rain coming down: "Achebe, Wren. Topside. Keep, nil. Short eleven seconds at the Caller, freely given."

"You could round it," Wren said.

"I've never rounded anything in my life," Quill said. "It's the only thing I'm good at."

Wren's hand was already inside her coat. She got the drowned slate out — the one she'd dredged off Ivo Salas, four plays left in it — and put her thumb to the corner where the margin lived, the private column, the place where she wrote down what people had done before she decided what they'd be allowed to remember. Her thumb went up the margin and found the top of it.

There was nothing on the page. Not full. Empty, and the wrong kind of empty. In eleven years she had logged every hour she'd ever rebuilt, every slate, every shift, because a thing written down can be picked back up and softened. She'd never logged the eleven seconds. That was the point of them. They had been the one item on the coast that existed nowhere but behind her own eyes.

They didn't exist there now either.

"Nothing to write in," she said.

"Then there's nothing to write," Quill said, not unkindly, which was worse. "That's not my doing. That's arithmetic."

Nia had turned to the rail with the orange wand against her ribs. Ivo Salas moved his hand an inch along the rope, the way a man does when he has something to say and fourteen months have taken the place he kept it in.

Above the arch the bell-tower rope swung, and the hammer came up out of its notch and stood there.

"Bayo," Sol said.

"That's the chain out at the next pull," Bayo said. "One toll. That's the lot."

"Eighty-one," Mara said pleasantly, into the rain. "Somebody's rope."

Quill came round the crate with the book flat to her chest against the rain and stopped in front of the old diver at the lift-frame. She didn't ask him anything. Wren watched her not ask, and watched the deck clock it too.

"You'll want his name out of his own mouth," Wren said. "Same as hers."

"His name's not a stranger's to me." Quill turned the book so the lantern fell on a page further back, and there it was in older ink, a name with a stroke drawn clean through it. "Fourteen months ago this man went down my bell on a night dive, and his line came up cut and he didn't come up with it. I closed him myself. Wrote *Ivo Salas* and struck it, because that's what you do with the ones the water's got." She set the pencil to a fresh line and wrote it again, whole. "I'm not taking a name off a coat-hook or out of a rumour. I'm putting back one I struck out with my own hand. The rule's for names I've never had. This one I've already paid for."

Nobody said anything to that. At the rail Bayo looked at the black water and kept his bandaged hands where they were.

The pencil went on to the third column and hung there. "Keep."

"Nothing," Wren said. "He came up hollow. Not a figure of speech — below the Line the cold gets into the part that holds on to things, and he stayed under past it, and he spent the hours he had left handing his air to somebody down in the dark. They don't grow back. He held his own name through all of it and lost everything hung either side of it." She heard her own voice go flat and even, the topside voice, the one she used on the bereaved. "Nil's the honest word."

Quill wrote *nil.* It was a short word and it cost her the length of a toll to get it down.

Then she looked up, and she looked at the two of them together — the diver who'd carried his name up out of fourteen months of black water and nothing else, and the woman lashed in the frame counting a rope that wasn't there — and something in the warden's face came loose that had been bolted there a long while.

She had never been below the Line. She'd stood at this counter and told dripping divers to their faces that they came up light because they'd gone down careless, and she'd believed it, because you believe the thing you've never had cause to test. She had the test open under her lantern now. Breathing. Upright. Empty. And not one bit of it careless.

She couldn't round it and she couldn't sit on it, so she did the only thing she'd ever been any good at. She said it plain, and she wrote it in her own hand in the open space below the columns, where a warden puts down the thing she'll answer for.

"Lost memory was never carelessness," Quill said. "I've said the reverse at this counter for years and I'll not carry it up the hill."

Then she turned the book to Mara, and the pencil came up, and the rule she'd just quoted turned its whole weight around and leaned on the one name it was actually for.

"Eighty-two," Mara said, pleasant as weather, watching the chains. "Somebody's rope."

"Mara." Quill didn't raise her voice; she never had to. "On the record. Your name, out of your own mouth, and I'll write your line and have you up out of this basin before that plate comes down. But it's yours to give. I'll not lift it off your daughter and I'll not invent it to save my berth."

Out past the arch the grate hung a hand's width over the black water, and the hammer stood up out of its notch, waiting on the last toll.

Nia let go of the rail.

She had the wand in her fist, orange gone the brown of a rusted hinge, and she carried it across the stage because her hand had held it a year and didn't know how to be empty. She knelt in the rain at the lift-frame, took her mother's face in both hands and turned it off the chains.

"Not the rope. Me."

"Somebody's rope," Mara said, and looked at her, pleasant as weather.

"There's one blank line left in the Kettle and I'm standing in front of it. You gave the deep your air and your hours and I've had fourteen months of not knowing, and I'm not doing this last one for you. Take it back off me." Nia's voice stayed level, which on her was the loud setting. "*Mara.*"

The pencil did not move.

"You told me she sang," Nia said, to Salas, without turning round.

Salas stood at the frame with one hand on the rope and said nothing. He'd said nothing since the Stair, and the rain went past him like he was a doorway.

So Wren got the drowned slate out of her coat. Four plays left in it; she'd counted them that morning the way another woman counts money. She thumbed the third one and turned it up to the deck.

Salas's voice came out cracked in the middle, the way an air valve cracks when a man has spent fourteen months opening it for somebody else. Two notes. Nothing else. Two notes, a breath, and the tick of a scrubber working.

Mara's mouth moved. Two notes, same pitch, same place in the breath.

"There's your song," Wren said. "It's the Caller's note. The bell rings it at slack water and it carries a long way through cold, and he was sat at forty-two metres for fourteen months with nothing else coming down to him. A man that far under doesn't keep the true shape of a thing, he keeps the nearest one he's got." She thumbed it off. "There was never a song. There was a bell and a man listening to it."

Nia looked at her mother's mouth a moment longer.

"Then it's in the bell and it can stay in the bell," she said. "I've one wand left and it's gone brown. I'm not spending my voice on a noise."

"Eighty-three," Mara said. Then she stopped. Her mouth worked twice on nothing, the way a pump does when it's lost its prime, and the third time it came out level and unhurried, four syllables in a row.

"Mara Vos."

Quill wrote fast, for her. "A name out of its own mouth is a name. I don't ask how it got there and I won't ask again." The pencil ran the line and turned the column. "*Vos, Mara. Diver. Keep, nil.*"

"Berth," Sol said.

"Four-eleven. High tier, dry, two doors off a standpipe." Quill read the whole line back flat, the way she read everything, then shut the book on her hand to keep the rain off it. "That's my count full, and it was full up before that plate moved."

"Nil's a hard word to live next to," Wren said.

"It's the true one and I've written it, so it's hers now, not mine." Quill looked past Nia at the deck. "The boy. I said I'd have him at this counter before I close, and I'll not have it said a warden of the Kettle shut a book on a family she hadn't finished counting."

"No," Nia said.

Under their feet the cabin hatch lifted.
